title: Discrete Mathematics — Concepts
intro:
## Discrete Mathematics (GATE CSE)

Covers the four syllabus blocks: **Mathematical Logic**, **Set Theory** (sets, relations, functions, posets, lattices, monoids, groups), **Graph Theory** and **Combinatorics**.

- Use the chapter tabs above to move between topics.
- Each chapter ends with a short set of practice questions for quick revision.
- Answers here are not counted on the dashboard; use the Practice, DPP and PYQ pages for tracked progress.

sections.title: Mathematical Logic — Propositional Logic
sections.summary: Connectives, equivalences, normal forms, tautology, functional completeness, inference.
sections.content:
## 1. Connectives and truth values

| $p$ | $q$ | $\neg p$ | $p\wedge q$ | $p\vee q$ | $p\to q$ | $p\leftrightarrow q$ | $p\oplus q$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| T | T | F | T | T | T | T | F |
| T | F | F | F | T | **F** | F | T |
| F | T | T | F | T | T | F | T |
| F | F | T | F | F | T | T | F |

$p\to q$ is false **only** when $p=T,\ q=F$.

## 2. Important equivalences

- $p\to q\equiv\neg p\vee q\equiv\neg q\to\neg p$ (contrapositive)
- Converse $q\to p$ and inverse $\neg p\to\neg q$ are equivalent to each other, **not** to $p\to q$
- $\neg(p\to q)\equiv p\wedge\neg q$
- De Morgan: $\neg(p\wedge q)\equiv\neg p\vee\neg q$, $\neg(p\vee q)\equiv\neg p\wedge\neg q$
- $p\leftrightarrow q\equiv(p\to q)\wedge(q\to p)\equiv\neg(p\oplus q)$
- Absorption: $p\vee(p\wedge q)\equiv p$, $p\wedge(p\vee q)\equiv p$
- Distributive: $p\wedge(q\vee r)\equiv(p\wedge q)\vee(p\wedge r)$ and vice versa

## 3. Tautology, contradiction, satisfiability

- **Tautology**: true in every row. **Contradiction**: false in every row. **Contingency**: neither.
- **Satisfiable**: true in at least one row. $\alpha$ is a tautology iff $\neg\alpha$ is unsatisfiable.
- With $n$ variables there are $2^n$ rows and $2^{2^n}$ distinct Boolean functions.

## 4. Normal forms and functional completeness

- DNF: OR of ANDs (minterms). CNF: AND of ORs (maxterms).
- Complete sets: $\{\wedge,\neg\}$, $\{\vee,\neg\}$, $\{\to,\neg\}$, $\{\uparrow\}$ (NAND), $\{\downarrow\}$ (NOR).
- **Not** complete: $\{\wedge,\vee\}$ and $\{\to\}$ alone (they cannot express negation).

## 5. Rules of inference

- Modus ponens: $p,\ p\to q\ \therefore q$
- Modus tollens: $\neg q,\ p\to q\ \therefore\neg p$
- Hypothetical syllogism: $p\to q,\ q\to r\ \therefore p\to r$
- Disjunctive syllogism: $p\vee q,\ \neg p\ \therefore q$
- Resolution: $p\vee q,\ \neg p\vee r\ \therefore q\vee r$
- Fallacies: affirming the consequent ($q,\ p\to q\ \therefore p$) and denying the antecedent are **invalid**.

**Exam tip (Hinglish):** Implication wale sawaal me pehle $p\to q$ ko $\neg p\vee q$ bana lo, fir sab simple ho jata hai.
keyPoints: NAND and NOR alone are functionally complete
Converse is not equivalent to the original implication

The contrapositive $

questions.title: Tautology
questions.question: Which of the following is a tautology?
questions.solution: This is modus ponens: whenever $p$ and $p\to q$ are true, $q$ is true, so the implication is always true. For (B) take $p=F,q=T$; for (C) take $p=F,q=T$ ($p\to q$ true, $q\to p$ false); (D) is a contradiction.

questions.title: Boolean functions
questions.question: The number of distinct Boolean functions of 3 variables is ______.
questions.solution: There are $2^3=8$ input rows and each can map to 0 or 1, so $2^8=256$.

questions.title: Functional completeness
questions.question: Which of the following sets of connectives are functionally complete?
questions.solution: NAND and NOR are each complete, and so is $\{\wedge,\neg\}$. $\{\wedge,\vee\}$ cannot express negation (it is monotone).

sections.title: Mathematical Logic — First Order Logic
sections.summary: Predicates, quantifiers, negation, translation of English, quantifier order.
sections.content:
## 1. Predicates and quantifiers

A predicate $P(x)$ becomes a proposition once $x$ is bound by a quantifier.

- $\forall x\,P(x)$: true iff $P(a)$ holds for **every** $a$ in the domain.
- $\exists x\,P(x)$: true iff $P(a)$ holds for **at least one** $a$.
- Over an **empty** domain $\forall x\,P(x)$ is true and $\exists x\,P(x)$ is false.

## 2. Negation (quantifier De Morgan)

- $\neg\forall x\,P(x)\equiv\exists x\,\neg P(x)$
- $\neg\exists x\,P(x)\equiv\forall x\,\neg P(x)$
- $\neg\forall x\,(P(x)\to Q(x))\equiv\exists x\,(P(x)\wedge\neg Q(x))$

## 3. Translating English (the classic traps)

| Sentence | Formula |
|---|---|
| All $S$ are $P$ | $\forall x\,(S(x)\to P(x))$ |
| Some $S$ are $P$ | $\exists x\,(S(x)\wedge P(x))$ |
| No $S$ is $P$ | $\forall x\,(S(x)\to\neg P(x))\equiv\neg\exists x\,(S(x)\wedge P(x))$ |
| Some $S$ are not $P$ | $\exists x\,(S(x)\wedge\neg P(x))$ |

- **Never** pair $\forall$ with $\wedge$ or $\exists$ with $\to$ for these patterns: $\forall x\,(S(x)\wedge P(x))$ says *everything* is an $S$, and $\exists x\,(S(x)\to P(x))$ is true whenever something is not an $S$.

## 4. Order of quantifiers

- Same type can be swapped: $\forall x\forall y\equiv\forall y\forall x$ and $\exists x\exists y\equiv\exists y\exists x$.
- Mixed type **cannot** be swapped. $\exists y\,\forall x\,P(x,y)\ \Rightarrow\ \forall x\,\exists y\,P(x,y)$ but **not** the converse.
- $\forall x\,(P\wedge Q)\equiv\forall x\,P\wedge\forall x\,Q$ and $\exists x\,(P\vee Q)\equiv\exists x\,P\vee\exists x\,Q$.
- $\forall x\,P\vee\forall x\,Q\Rightarrow\forall x\,(P\vee Q)$ but not conversely; $\exists x\,(P\wedge Q)\Rightarrow\exists x\,P\wedge\exists x\,Q$ but not conversely.

## 5. Validity

A first-order formula is **valid** if true in every interpretation. Validity of FOL is undecidable (but semi-decidable); satisfiability of propositional formulas is NP-complete.

**Exam tip (Hinglish):** "Sab ke liye" ke saath implication ($\to$), "kuch ke liye" ke saath AND ($\wedge$). Ulta likha to option galat.
keyPoints: $\exists y\forall x\Rightarrow\forall x\exists y$, not the converse

questions.title: Translation
questions.question: Which formula says "No student is lazy"? ($S$: student, $L$: lazy)
questions.solution: No student is lazy means there is no $x$ that is both a student and lazy: $\neg\exists x(S(x)\wedge L(x))\equiv\forall x(S(x)\to\neg L(x))$.

questions.title: Quantifier order
questions.question: Which statement is always true for every predicate $P$?
questions.solution: If one $y$ works for all $x$, then each $x$ certainly has some $y$. The converse fails: with $P(x,y):x<y$ over the integers, $\forall x\exists y$ is true but $\exists y\forall x$ is false.

questions.title: Translation
questions.question: Which formula expresses "every natural number has a larger natural number"?
questions.solution: For each $x$ there must exist a $y$ larger than it: $\forall x\,\exists y\,(y>x)$.

questions.title: Equivalences
questions.question: Which of the following are logically valid (true under all interpretations)?
questions.solution: (A) and (B) are valid. (C) fails when $P$ and $Q$ each hold for different elements: the right side is true but both $\forall x P$ and $\forall x Q$ are false. (D) fails when different elements satisfy $P$ and $Q$.

sections.title: Set Theory — Sets and Relations
sections.summary: Set identities, power set, relation properties and counting, equivalence relations, closures.
sections.content:
## 1. Sets

- $|A\cup B|=|A|+|B|-|A\cap B|$. For three sets use inclusion–exclusion.
- $|\mathcal P(A)|=2^{|A|}$. $|A\times B|=|A||B|$.
- De Morgan: $\overline{A\cup B}=\overline A\cap\overline B$.
- $A\setminus B=A\cap\overline B$; symmetric difference $A\oplus B=(A\setminus B)\cup(B\setminus A)$.

## 2. Relations and their properties

A relation $R$ on $A$ is a subset of $A\times A$.

| Property | Condition |
|---|---|
| Reflexive | $(a,a)\in R$ for all $a$ |
| Irreflexive | $(a,a)\notin R$ for all $a$ |
| Symmetric | $(a,b)\in R\Rightarrow(b,a)\in R$ |
| Antisymmetric | $(a,b),(b,a)\in R\Rightarrow a=b$ |
| Transitive | $(a,b),(b,c)\in R\Rightarrow(a,c)\in R$ |

- **Equivalence** = reflexive + symmetric + transitive. It partitions $A$ into equivalence classes.
- **Partial order** = reflexive + antisymmetric + transitive.
- Symmetric and antisymmetric are not opposites; the identity relation is both. The empty relation is symmetric, antisymmetric and transitive.

## 3. Counting relations on an $n$-element set

| Type | Count |
|---|---|
| All relations | $2^{n^2}$ |
| Reflexive | $2^{n^2-n}$ |
| Symmetric | $2^{n(n+1)/2}$ |
| Antisymmetric | $2^n\cdot3^{n(n-1)/2}$ |
| Asymmetric | $3^{n(n-1)/2}$ |
| Equivalence relations | Bell number $B_n$: $1,2,5,15,52,203,\dots$ |

## 4. Composition and closures

- $R\circ S=\{(a,c):\exists b,\ (a,b)\in S,\ (b,c)\in R\}$ (check the convention used in the question).
- Reflexive closure $R\cup I$; symmetric closure $R\cup R^{-1}$; transitive closure $R^+=R\cup R^2\cup\dots\cup R^n$ (Warshall's algorithm, $O(n^3)$).
- Congruence mod $m$ is an equivalence relation with $m$ classes.

**Exam tip (Hinglish):** Relation ke properties check karte waqt chhote counter-example (jaise $(1,2)$ aur $(2,1)$) se jaldi decide ho jata hai.
keyPoints: Equivalence relations on $n$ elements = Bell number $B_n$

questions.title: Reflexive relations
questions.question: The number of reflexive relations on a set with 3 elements is ______.
questions.solution: All 3 pairs $(a,a)$ are forced; each of the remaining $9-3=6$ pairs is free: $2^6=64$.

questions.title: Symmetric relations
questions.question: The number of symmetric relations on a set of 4 elements is ______.
questions.solution: A symmetric relation is determined by the 4 diagonal pairs and the $\binom42=6$ unordered off-diagonal pairs: $2^{4+6}=2^{10}=1024$.

questions.title: Equivalence relations
questions.question: The number of equivalence relations on a set of 4 elements is ______.
questions.solution: This is the number of partitions of a 4-set, the Bell number $B_4=15$.

questions.title: Antisymmetric relations
questions.question: The number of antisymmetric relations on a set with 3 elements is ______.

questions.title: Properties
questions.question: $R=\{(1,1),(2,2),(1,2),(2,1)\}$ on $\{1,2,3\}$ is
options: symmetric and transitive but not reflexive
reflexive and symmetric but not transitive
questions.solution: $(3,3)\notin R$, so it is not reflexive. It is symmetric, and it is transitive (all compositions stay inside $\{1,2\}^2$). It is not antisymmetric since $(1,2),(2,1)\in R$.

questions.title: Congruence
questions.question: The number of equivalence classes of the relation $a\equiv b\pmod 5$ on the integers is
questions.solution: Residues $0,1,2,3,4$ give exactly 5 classes.

sections.title: Set Theory — Functions
sections.summary: Injective, surjective, bijective, composition, inverse and counting functions.
sections.content:
## 1. Types of functions $f:A\to B$

- **Injective (one-one)**: $f(a)=f(b)\Rightarrow a=b$.
- **Surjective (onto)**: every $b\in B$ has some $a$ with $f(a)=b$.
- **Bijective**: both. Only bijections have an inverse $f^{-1}$.

## 2. Counting with $|A|=m$, $|B|=n$

| Kind | Count |
|---|---|
| All functions | $n^m$ |
| Injective | $P(n,m)=\dfrac{n!}{(n-m)!}$ (needs $m\le n$) |
| Bijective | $n!$ if $m=n$ |
| Surjective | $\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{n}(-1)^k\binom nk(n-k)^m$ (needs $m\ge n$) |

Example: onto functions from a 4-set to a 3-set $=3^4-3\cdot2^4+3\cdot1^4=36$.

## 3. Composition

- $(g\circ f)(x)=g(f(x))$. Composition is associative, not commutative.
- If $g\circ f$ is injective then $f$ is injective.
- If $g\circ f$ is surjective then $g$ is surjective.
- Composition of bijections is a bijection, and $(g\circ f)^{-1}=f^{-1}\circ g^{-1}$.

## 4. Finite sets and cardinality

- For $|A|=|B|$ finite: injective $\iff$ surjective $\iff$ bijective.
- $f:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z$, $f(x)=x^2$ is neither injective nor surjective; $f(x)=2x$ is injective but not surjective; $f(x)=x+1$ is bijective.
- $\mathbb N,\mathbb Z,\mathbb Q$ are countable; $\mathbb R$ and $\mathcal P(\mathbb N)$ are uncountable.
- Pigeonhole: no injection from a larger finite set to a smaller one.

**Exam tip (Hinglish):** Onto functions ka count yaad nahi to inclusion–exclusion formula likh do, 2-3 lines me ho jata hai.

questions.title: Onto functions
questions.question: The number of onto (surjective) functions from a set of 4 elements to a set of 3 elements is ______.

questions.title: Injective functions
questions.question: The number of one-one functions from a 3-element set to a 5-element set is ______.
questions.solution: $5\cdot4\cdot3=60$.

questions.title: Type of function
questions.question: The function $f:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z$, $f(x)=x^2$ is
questions.solution: $f(2)=f(-2)$ so it is not injective, and negative integers are never attained, so it is not surjective.

questions.title: Composition
questions.question: If $g\circ f:A\to C$ is injective, then which of the following must be true?
questions.solution: If $f(a)=f(b)$ then $g(f(a))=g(f(b))$, hence $a=b$. So $f$ must be injective; $g$ need not be.

questions.title: Counting functions
questions.question: The number of functions from $\{1,2,3\}$ to $\{1,2,3,4\}$ is ______.
questions.solution: Each of the 3 elements has 4 choices: $4^3=64.$

sections.title: Set Theory — Partial Orders and Lattices
sections.summary: Hasse diagrams, extremal elements, lub/glb, lattices, Boolean lattices, chains and antichains.
sections.content:
## 1. Partial orders and Hasse diagrams

A **poset** $(P,\preceq)$ is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive. The Hasse diagram omits self-loops, transitive edges and arrow directions (lower elements are drawn lower).

- **Maximal / minimal**: no element strictly above / below it (can be several).
- **Greatest / least**: above / below **all** elements (unique if it exists).
- **Upper bound / lower bound** of a subset $S$; **lub** = least upper bound (join, $\vee$), **glb** = greatest lower bound (meet, $\wedge$).
- **Chain**: every two elements comparable. **Antichain**: no two comparable.
- **Dilworth**: minimum number of chains covering a poset = size of the largest antichain.

## 2. Lattices

A poset is a **lattice** if every pair $\{a,b\}$ has both a lub and a glb. Every finite lattice has a greatest ($1$) and least ($0$) element.

- **Bounded** (has $0$ and $1$), **complemented** (each $a$ has $a'$ with $a\vee a'=1,\ a\wedge a'=0$), **distributive** ($a\wedge(b\vee c)=(a\wedge b)\vee(a\wedge c)$).
- A lattice is non-distributive iff it contains the diamond $M_3$ or pentagon $N_5$ as a sublattice.
- In a distributive lattice, complements are **unique** when they exist.
- **Boolean lattice** = complemented distributive lattice with $0,1$. A finite Boolean lattice has $2^n$ elements and is isomorphic to $(\mathcal P(\{1..n\}),\subseteq)$.

## 3. Standard examples

- $(\mathcal P(S),\subseteq)$: join = union, meet = intersection; Boolean.
- $(\mathbb N,\mid)$ or $D_n$ (divisors of $n$ under divisibility): join = lcm, meet = gcd. $D_n$ is Boolean iff $n$ is **square-free**; it has $d(n)$ elements, e.g. $D_{30}$ has 8.
- $(\mathbb Z,\le)$ is a chain and a distributive lattice but not bounded.
- Hasse diagram of $\mathcal P(\{a,b,c\})$ is a cube: 8 nodes, 12 edges, 6 maximal chains ($3!$).

**Exam tip (Hinglish):** Lattice sawaal me pehle dekho har pair ka lub aur glb exist karta hai ya nahi. Square-free wala trick $D_n$ ke liye bahut kaam aata hai.
keyPoints: Lattice: every pair has lub and glb
Hasse diagram of $\mathcal P(\{a,b,c\})$ has 12 edges

questions.title: Elements of D30
questions.question: The number of elements in the lattice $D_{30}$ (divisors of 30 under divisibility) is ______.
questions.solution: $30=2\cdot3\cdot5$ has $2^3=8$ divisors, and $D_{30}$ is the Boolean lattice on 3 atoms.

questions.title: Boolean lattice
questions.question: Which of the following divisor lattices is a Boolean lattice?
questions.solution: $D_n$ is Boolean iff $n$ is square-free. $30=2\cdot3\cdot5$ is square-free; $12=2^2\cdot3$, $18=2\cdot3^2$ and $36=2^2\cdot3^2$ are not.

questions.title: lub in divisibility
questions.question: In the poset $(\mathbb N,\mid)$, the least upper bound of $4$ and $6$ is
questions.solution: Under divisibility the lub is the lcm: $\mathrm{lcm}(4,6)=12$.

questions.title: Hasse diagram of subsets
questions.question: The number of edges in the Hasse diagram of $(\mathcal P(\{a,b,c\}),\subseteq)$ is ______.
questions.solution: It is the 3-cube: each of the 8 subsets of size $k$ covers $k$ subsets, so edges $=0+1+1+1+2+2+2+3=12$ (equivalently $3\cdot2^2$).

questions.title: Maximal chains
questions.question: The number of maximal chains in $(\mathcal P(\{a,b,c\}),\subseteq)$ from $\varnothing$ to $\{a,b,c\}$ is ______.
questions.solution: Each maximal chain adds one element at a time, so it corresponds to an ordering of $a,b,c$: $3!=6$.

questions.title: Lattice facts
questions.question: Which of the following statements are true?
options: Every finite lattice has a greatest and a least element
Every chain is a distributive lattice
In a distributive lattice a complement, if it exists, is unique
questions.solution: A finite lattice is bounded by the join and meet of all its elements; any chain is a lattice with $\max$ and $\min$ and is distributive; uniqueness of complements holds in distributive lattices. Not every lattice is distributive ($M_3,N_5$).

sections.title: Set Theory — Monoids and Groups
sections.summary: Algebraic structures, subgroups, cyclic groups, order of elements and Lagrange's theorem.
sections.content:
## 1. Hierarchy of algebraic structures

| Structure | Axioms |
|---|---|
| Closure / groupoid | $a*b\in S$ |
| **Semigroup** | closure + associativity |
| **Monoid** | semigroup + identity |
| **Group** | monoid + every element has an inverse |
| Abelian group | group + commutativity |

Examples: $(\mathbb N,+)$ is a monoid (identity 0) but not a group; $(\mathbb Z,+)$ is an abelian group; $(\mathbb Z,-)$ is not even a semigroup (not associative); $(\mathbb Z_n,+_n)$ is a cyclic group; $(\mathbb Z_p^*,\times_p)$ is a group iff $p$ is prime; $(\mathbb Z_n^*,\times_n)$ has $\varphi(n)$ elements.

## 2. Basic facts

- Identity and inverses are **unique**. $(ab)^{-1}=b^{-1}a^{-1}$.
- Cancellation laws hold. Every row/column of the Cayley table is a permutation.
- A group of **even order** has an element of order 2. A group in which every $a^2=e$ is abelian.

## 3. Subgroups and Lagrange

- $H\subseteq G$ is a subgroup iff $H\ne\varnothing$ and $a,b\in H\Rightarrow ab^{-1}\in H$ (for finite $H$: closure suffices).
- **Lagrange**: $|H|$ divides $|G|$. Hence the order of every element divides $|G|$, and a group of **prime** order is cyclic with no proper non-trivial subgroups.
- The converse of Lagrange is false: $A_4$ (order 12) has no subgroup of order 6.
- Intersection of subgroups is a subgroup; union generally is not.

## 4. Cyclic groups and orders

- $G=\langle g\rangle$. The order of $a$ in $\mathbb Z_n$ (addition) is $\dfrac{n}{\gcd(a,n)}$.
- A cyclic group of order $n$ has exactly $\varphi(n)$ generators, and exactly one subgroup for each divisor of $n$.
- Every cyclic group is abelian; every subgroup of a cyclic group is cyclic.
- $|ab|=|a||b|$ only when $a,b$ commute and $\gcd(|a|,|b|)=1$.

**Exam tip (Hinglish):** Group ka order divisors se hi subgroup order ban sakta hai. Option me aisa number ho jo order ko divide nahi karta, wahi galat hai.
keyPoints: Monoid has identity but no inverses
Cyclic group of order $n$ has $\varphi(n)$ generators
Group of prime order is cyclic

questions.title: Order of an element
questions.question: The order of the element $3$ in the group $(\mathbb Z_{12},+_{12})$ is ______.

questions.title: Generators
questions.question: The number of generators of the cyclic group $\mathbb Z_{12}$ is ______.
questions.solution: $\varphi(12)=4$ (the generators are $1,5,7,11$).

questions.title: Lagrange
questions.question: Which of the following cannot be the order of a subgroup of a group of order 12?
questions.solution: By Lagrange the order of a subgroup divides 12. $5$ does not divide 12.

questions.title: Monoid vs group
questions.question: Which of the following is a monoid but not a group?
questions.solution: $(\mathbb N\cup\{0\},+)$ is associative with identity 0, but $1$ has no additive inverse in the set.

questions.title: Prime order
questions.question: A group of order 7 is
questions.solution: Any non-identity element has order dividing 7, hence order 7, and generates the group. So it is cyclic (hence abelian) with no subgroup of order 3.

sections.title: Graph Theory — Basics, Trees and Connectivity
sections.summary: Degrees, handshaking, trees, Euler and Hamilton paths, connectivity, bipartite graphs.
sections.content:
## 1. Basics

- **Handshaking**: $\sum_v\deg(v)=2|E|$. The number of odd-degree vertices is even.
- Simple graph on $n$ vertices has at most $\binom n2$ edges ($K_n$). $K_n$ is $(n-1)$-regular.
- $K_{m,n}$ has $mn$ edges. A bipartite graph on $n$ vertices has at most $\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor$ edges.
- A graph is **bipartite iff it has no odd cycle**.
- Degree sequence is graphical iff it passes Havel–Hakimi.

## 2. Trees

For a graph $G$ with $n$ vertices, the following are equivalent for a tree: connected and acyclic $\iff$ connected with $n-1$ edges $\iff$ acyclic with $n-1$ edges $\iff$ exactly one path between each pair.

- A forest with $n$ vertices and $k$ components has $n-k$ edges.
- Every tree with $n\ge2$ has at least 2 leaves. Number of leaves $=2+\sum_{\deg\ge3}(\deg-2)$.
- **Cayley**: number of labelled trees on $n$ vertices (= spanning trees of $K_n$) is $n^{n-2}$.
- Spanning tree of a connected graph: $n-1$ edges; the number of non-tree edges is $|E|-n+1$ (cyclomatic number).

## 3. Euler and Hamilton

- **Euler circuit** (uses every edge once, returns): connected and all degrees even.
- **Euler path** (not closed): connected with exactly 0 or 2 odd-degree vertices.
- **Hamiltonian cycle** (every vertex once): no simple necessary-and-sufficient test (NP-complete). Sufficient: **Dirac** $\deg(v)\ge n/2$ for all $v$ ($n\ge3$); **Ore** $\deg u+\deg v\ge n$ for non-adjacent pairs.
- $K_n$ ($n\ge3$) is Hamiltonian; it is Eulerian iff $n$ is odd.

## 4. Connectivity

- **Cut vertex** / **bridge**: removal disconnects the graph.
- Vertex connectivity $\kappa(G)\le$ edge connectivity $\lambda(G)\le\delta(G)$ (Whitney).
- $K_n$: $\kappa=n-1$. $C_n$: $\kappa=\lambda=2$. Tree: $\lambda=1$.
- A connected graph with $n$ vertices has at least $n-1$ edges.

**Exam tip (Hinglish):** Euler wale sawaal me sirf degrees dekho (sab even?) aur connectivity. Hamilton ke liye Dirac/Ore sirf sufficient hai, necessary nahi.
keyPoints: Euler circuit: connected and all degrees even

questions.title: Handshaking
questions.question: The number of edges in a 4-regular graph on 10 vertices is ______.

questions.title: Spanning trees of K5
questions.question: The number of distinct labelled spanning trees of $K_5$ is ______.
questions.solution: Cayley's formula: $5^{5-2}=125$.

questions.title: Forest
questions.question: A forest has 20 vertices and 4 connected components. The number of edges is ______.
questions.solution: A forest with $n$ vertices and $k$ components has $n-k=16$ edges.

questions.title: Euler circuit
questions.question: Which of the following complete graphs has an Euler circuit?
questions.solution: $K_n$ is $(n-1)$-regular; all degrees are even only when $n$ is odd. Among the options only $K_5$ qualifies.

questions.title: Leaves of a tree
questions.question: A tree has exactly one vertex of degree 4, one vertex of degree 3, and all other vertices are leaves. The number of leaves is ______.
questions.solution: Let there be $L$ leaves, so $n=L+2$ and $\sum\deg=4+3+L=2(n-1)=2(L+1)$. Hence $L=5$.

questions.title: Bipartite
questions.question: A graph is bipartite if and only if it
questions.solution: This is König's characterization: bipartite $\iff$ every cycle has even length.

sections.title: Graph Theory — Matching, Colouring and Planarity
sections.summary: Matchings, Hall's theorem, chromatic number, planar graphs, Euler's formula.
sections.content:
## 1. Matching

- A **matching** is a set of edges with no common vertex. **Perfect matching** covers every vertex (needs even $n$).
- **Hall's theorem**: a bipartite graph $(X,Y)$ has a matching saturating $X$ iff $|N(S)|\ge|S|$ for every $S\subseteq X$.
- **König**: in a bipartite graph, maximum matching size = minimum vertex cover size.
- $K_{m,n}$ has maximum matching $\min(m,n)$. $K_{n}$ ($n$ even) has a perfect matching. Every $k$-regular bipartite graph ($k\ge1$) has a perfect matching.
- Independence number $\alpha$, vertex cover $\beta$: $\alpha+\beta=n$ in every graph.

## 2. Colouring

- **Chromatic number** $\chi(G)$: least number of colours for a proper vertex colouring.
- $\chi(K_n)=n$; $\chi(\text{bipartite})=2$ (with at least one edge); $\chi(C_n)=2$ if $n$ even, $3$ if $n$ odd; $\chi(\text{tree})=2$.
- $\omega(G)\le\chi(G)\le\Delta(G)+1$. **Brooks**: $\chi\le\Delta$ unless $G$ is complete or an odd cycle.
- **Four colour theorem**: every planar graph is 4-colourable.
- Wheel $W_n$ (hub + $C_n$): $\chi=3$ if $n$ even, $4$ if $n$ odd.
- Chromatic polynomial of a tree on $n$ vertices is $k(k-1)^{n-1}$; of $K_n$ is $k(k-1)\cdots(k-n+1)$.
- Edge chromatic number: $\Delta$ or $\Delta+1$ (Vizing); bipartite graphs have $\chi'=\Delta$.

## 3. Planar graphs

- **Euler's formula** (connected planar): $V-E+F=2$.
- Simple connected planar, $V\ge3$: $E\le3V-6$. If also triangle-free (e.g. bipartite): $E\le2V-4$.
- Every planar graph has a vertex of degree $\le5$.
- **Kuratowski**: planar iff no subdivision of $K_5$ or $K_{3,3}$. Both $K_5$ and $K_{3,3}$ are non-planar.
- For a connected planar graph with all faces bounded by at least $g$ edges: $E\le\dfrac{g}{g-2}(V-2)$.

**Exam tip (Hinglish):** Planar graph me $V,E,F$ ka sawaal ho to seedha $V-E+F=2$. Max edges poochhe to $3V-6$ (ya bipartite me $2V-4$).
keyPoints: König: max matching = min vertex cover (bipartite)

questions.title: Euler's formula
questions.question: A connected planar graph has 10 vertices and 15 edges. The number of faces (including the outer face) is ______.

questions.title: Maximum planar edges
questions.question: The maximum number of edges in a simple planar graph with 6 vertices is ______.
questions.solution: $E\le3V-6=12$ (attained by the octahedron).

questions.title: Chromatic number
questions.question: The chromatic number of the wheel graph with a hub and a cycle $C_5$ (6 vertices) is ______.
questions.solution: The $C_5$ needs 3 colours (odd cycle), and the hub is adjacent to all rim vertices, so a 4th colour is needed.

questions.title: Maximum matching
questions.question: The size of a maximum matching in $K_{4,6}$ is ______.
questions.solution: For $K_{m,n}$ the maximum matching has $\min(m,n)=4$ edges.

questions.title: Non-planar graph
questions.question: Which of the following graphs is NOT planar?
questions.solution: $K_5$ has $E=10>3V-6=9$, so it is non-planar.

questions.title: Chromatic polynomial
questions.question: The number of proper colourings of a path on 4 vertices using at most 3 colours is ______.

sections.title: Combinatorics — Counting
sections.summary: Permutations, combinations, stars and bars, inclusion–exclusion, derangements, pigeonhole.
sections.content:
## 1. Basic principles

- **Sum rule**: $m$ or $n$ ways (disjoint) $\Rightarrow m+n$. **Product rule**: $m$ then $n$ ways $\Rightarrow mn$.
- $P(n,r)=\dfrac{n!}{(n-r)!}$, $\ \binom nr=\dfrac{n!}{r!(n-r)!}$, $\ \binom nr=\binom n{n-r}$, Pascal: $\binom nr=\binom{n-1}{r-1}+\binom{n-1}r$.
- Circular arrangements of $n$ distinct objects: $(n-1)!$ (divide by 2 more if reflections are identical).
- Arrangements with repeated objects: $\dfrac{n!}{n_1!\,n_2!\cdots n_k!}$.

## 2. Selections with repetition (stars and bars)

- Non-negative solutions of $x_1+\dots+x_k=n$: $\dbinom{n+k-1}{k-1}$.
- Positive solutions ($x_i\ge1$): $\dbinom{n-1}{k-1}$.
- With lower bounds, substitute $y_i=x_i-\ell_i$ first.
- Multisets of size $r$ from $n$ types: $\dbinom{n+r-1}{r}$.

## 3. Binomial theorem and identities

- $(x+y)^n=\sum_{k}\binom nk x^{n-k}y^k$; $\sum_k\binom nk=2^n$; $\sum_k(-1)^k\binom nk=0$.
- $\sum_{k}\binom nk^2=\binom{2n}{n}$ (Vandermonde special case).
- Catalan $C_n=\dfrac1{n+1}\binom{2n}n$ counts balanced parentheses, binary trees with $n$ nodes, etc.

## 4. Inclusion–exclusion and derangements

- $|A_1\cup\dots\cup A_n|=\sum|A_i|-\sum|A_i\cap A_j|+\sum|A_i\cap A_j\cap A_k|-\dots$
- **Derangements**: $D_n=n!\sum_{k=0}^n\frac{(-1)^k}{k!}$, with $D_1=0,D_2=1,D_3=2,D_4=9,D_5=44$ and $D_n=(n-1)(D_{n-1}+D_{n-2})$.

## 5. Pigeonhole principle

- If $n$ items go into $k$ boxes, some box has at least $\lceil n/k\rceil$ items.
- To **guarantee** $r$ items in some box you need $k(r-1)+1$ items.

**Exam tip (Hinglish):** "Kam se kam ek" wale sawaal me total minus (koi nahi) try karo, inclusion–exclusion se pehle.

questions.title: Inclusion-exclusion
questions.question: The number of integers from 1 to 100 divisible by 2 or 3 is ______.
questions.solution: $\lfloor100/2\rfloor+\lfloor100/3\rfloor-\lfloor100/6\rfloor=50+33-16=67$.

questions.title: Pigeonhole
questions.question: The minimum number of people needed to guarantee that at least 2 of them were born in the same month is ______.
questions.solution: There are 12 months (boxes), so $12\cdot1+1=13$ people are needed.

sections.title: Combinatorics — Recurrence Relations
sections.summary: Setting up recurrences, solving linear homogeneous and non-homogeneous ones.
sections.content:
## 1. Linear recurrences with constant coefficients

$a_n=c_1a_{n-1}+c_2a_{n-2}+\dots+c_ka_{n-k}+f(n)$.

**Homogeneous** ($f=0$). Write the characteristic equation $r^k=c_1r^{k-1}+\dots+c_k$.

- Distinct roots $r_1,\dots,r_k$: $a_n=\alpha_1r_1^n+\dots+\alpha_kr_k^n$.
- A root $r$ of multiplicity $m$ contributes $(\beta_0+\beta_1n+\dots+\beta_{m-1}n^{m-1})\,r^n$.
- Constants come from the initial conditions.

Example: $a_n=5a_{n-1}-6a_{n-2}$, $a_0=1,\,a_1=1$. Roots $2,3$; $a_n=A2^n+B3^n$, with $A+B=1,\ 2A+3B=1$ giving $A=2,B=-1$, so $a_n=2^{n+1}-3^n$.

## 2. Non-homogeneous

$a_n=a_n^{(h)}+a_n^{(p)}$. Guess the particular solution from $f(n)$:

| $f(n)$ | Guess $a_n^{(p)}$ |
|---|---|
| constant $c$ | $A$ (use $An$ if $1$ is a root, $An^2$ if double root) |
| polynomial of degree $d$ | polynomial of degree $d$ (multiply by $n$ if $1$ is a root) |
| $c\cdot s^n$ | $A s^n$ (multiply by $n$ if $s$ is a root) |

## 3. Setting up recurrences (frequent GATE theme)

- **Tower of Hanoi**: $T(n)=2T(n-1)+1,\ T(1)=1\Rightarrow T(n)=2^n-1$.
- **Binary strings of length $n$ with no two consecutive 0s**: $f(n)=f(n-1)+f(n-2)$, $f(1)=2,\ f(2)=3$ (Fibonacci-like).
- **Fibonacci**: $F_n=F_{n-1}+F_{n-2}$ with closed form $F_n=\dfrac{\phi^n-\psi^n}{\sqrt5}$.
- **Divide and conquer**: $T(n)=aT(n/b)+f(n)$ solved by the Master theorem or by repeated substitution.
- Sum of first $n$ odd numbers: $T(n)=T(n-1)+2n-1\Rightarrow T(n)=n^2$.

**Exam tip (Hinglish):** Pehle characteristic roots nikalo. Repeated root ho to $n$ se multiply karna mat bhoolna.
keyPoints: Use initial conditions to find constants

questions.title: Repeated root
questions.question: The general solution of $a_n=4a_{n-1}-4a_{n-2}$ is
questions.solution: The characteristic equation $r^2-4r+4=0$ has a double root $r=2$, so the solution is $(A+Bn)2^n$.

questions.title: Tower of Hanoi
questions.question: The minimum number of moves for the Tower of Hanoi with 6 discs, given $T(n)=2T(n-1)+1$ and $T(1)=1$, is ______.

questions.title: Binary strings
questions.question: The number of binary strings of length 8 with no two consecutive 0s is ______.

questions.title: Sum recurrence
questions.question: $T(n)=T(n-1)+2n-1$ with $T(1)=1$. The value of $T(12)$ is ______.
questions.solution: $T(n)=n^2$ (sum of the first $n$ odd numbers), so $T(12)=144$.

sections.title: Combinatorics — Generating Functions
sections.summary: Ordinary generating functions, standard series, counting with bounds, solving recurrences.
sections.content:
## 1. Definition

The (ordinary) generating function of $\langle a_n\rangle$ is $A(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}a_nx^n$.

## 2. Standard series

| Sequence | $A(x)$ |
|---|---|
| $1,1,1,\dots$ | $\dfrac1{1-x}$ |
| $c^n$ | $\dfrac1{1-cx}$ |
| $n$ | $\dfrac{x}{(1-x)^2}$ |
| $\binom{n+k-1}{k-1}$ (coefficient of $x^n$ in) | $\dfrac1{(1-x)^k}$ |
| $\binom nk$ (finite) | $(1+x)^n$ |
| $1,1,\dots,1$ ($m$ ones) | $\dfrac{1-x^m}{1-x}$ |
| $\dfrac1{n!}$ | $e^x$ (exponential GF) |

## 3. Operations

- Sum: $A(x)+B(x)$. Shift right: $x\,A(x)$ gives $a_{n-1}$.
- **Convolution**: $A(x)B(x)$ has coefficients $c_n=\sum_{k}a_kb_{n-k}$.
- Partial sums: $\dfrac{A(x)}{1-x}$ has coefficients $a_0+\dots+a_n$.
- Differentiation: $x A'(x)$ gives $n\,a_n$.

## 4. Counting solutions with bounds

Number of solutions of $x_1+\dots+x_k=n$ with $0\le x_i\le m$ is the coefficient of $x^n$ in $\left(\dfrac{1-x^{m+1}}{1-x}\right)^k$.

Example ($k=3$, $m=5$, $n=12$): coefficient of $x^{12}$ in $(1-x^6)^3(1-x)^{-3}=\binom{14}{2}-3\binom82+3\binom22=91-84+3=10$.

## 5. Solving a recurrence

Multiply the recurrence by $x^n$, sum, solve for $A(x)$, use partial fractions and read off the coefficients. For $a_n=2a_{n-1},\ a_0=1$: $A(x)(1-2x)=1$, so $A(x)=\dfrac1{1-2x}$ and $a_n=2^n$.

**Exam tip (Hinglish):** "Coefficient of $x^n$" wale sawaal me $\frac1{(1-x)^k}$ ka formula yaad rakho, aur bound ho to $(1-x^{m+1})$ wala factor lagao.

questions.title: Standard GF
questions.question: The generating function of the sequence $a_n=2^n$ ($n\ge0$) is
questions.solution: $\sum2^nx^n=\sum(2x)^n=\dfrac1{1-2x}$.

questions.title: Coefficient
questions.question: The coefficient of $x^{10}$ in $\dfrac1{(1-x)^3}$ is ______.

questions.title: Bounded solutions
questions.question: The number of integer solutions of $x_1+x_2+x_3=12$ with $0\le x_i\le5$ is ______.
questions.solution: Substitute $y_i=5-x_i$: $y_1+y_2+y_3=3$ with $y_i\ge0$, giving $\binom{5}{2}=10$. (Equivalently, the inclusion–exclusion value $91-84+3=10$.)

questions.title: Sequence n
questions.question: The generating function of the sequence $0,1,2,3,\dots$ ($a_n=n$) is
questions.solution: Differentiate $\frac1{1-x}$ to get $\frac1{(1-x)^2}=\sum(n+1)x^n$, then multiply by $x$: $\sum nx^n=\frac{x}{(1-x)^2}$.

questions.title: Coefficient in a product
questions.question: The coefficient of $x^5$ in $(1+x+x^2)^3$ is ______.
questions.solution: $(1+x+x^2)^3=1+3x+6x^2+7x^3+6x^4+3x^5+x^6$, so the coefficient of $x^5$ is 3.
